statement: Prove that a subset U of a topological space is open if and only if it equals its own interior.
solution: int(U) is the union of all open sets contained in U, hence open and contained in U. If U=int(U) then U is open. Conversely if U is open then U is an open set contained in U, so U⊆int(U); combined with int(U)⊆U this gives equality.

statement: Prove that a subset A of a topological space is closed if and only if A equals its closure.
solution: cl(A) is the intersection of all closed sets containing A, hence closed, and A⊆cl(A). If A=cl(A) then A is closed. Conversely if A is closed then A is a closed set containing A, so cl(A)⊆A, giving A=cl(A).

statement: Prove that the interior of A is the largest open set contained in A.
solution: int(A)=union of all open subsets of A, so it is open (union of opens) and contained in A. Any open set G with G⊆A is one of the sets in that union, so G⊆int(A). Hence int(A) is the largest such set.

statement: Prove that x lies in the closure of A if and only if every open neighborhood of x intersects A.
solution: If some open nbhd U of x misses A, then X\U is closed, contains A, and excludes x, so x∉cl(A). Conversely if x∉cl(A), then X\cl(A) is an open nbhd of x disjoint from A. Contrapositive gives the equivalence.

statement: Prove that x is a limit point of A if and only if every open neighborhood of x contains a point of A different from x.
solution: This is the definition of a limit point: x∈cl(A\{x}). By the neighborhood characterization of closure, x∈cl(A\{x}) iff every open nbhd of x meets A\{x}, i.e. contains a point of A other than x.

statement: Prove that the boundary of a set A, defined as cl(A) ∩ cl(X\A), is closed.
solution: cl(A) and cl(X\A) are each closed by definition of closure. The intersection of two closed sets is closed, so ∂A=cl(A)∩cl(X\A) is closed.

statement: Prove that if A ⊆ B then cl(A) ⊆ cl(B).
solution: cl(B) is a closed set containing B, hence containing A. Since cl(A) is the smallest closed set containing A, cl(A)⊆cl(B).

statement: Prove that the closure operation is idempotent: cl(cl(A)) = cl(A).
solution: cl(A) is closed, and a set equals its closure iff it is closed (b02). Hence cl(cl(A))=cl(A).

statement: Prove that cl(A ∪ B) = cl(A) ∪ cl(B).
solution: cl(A)∪cl(B) is closed and contains A∪B, so cl(A∪B)⊆cl(A)∪cl(B). Conversely A⊆A∪B gives cl(A)⊆cl(A∪B) (b07), similarly for B, so cl(A)∪cl(B)⊆cl(A∪B). Hence equality.

statement: Prove that int(A ∩ B) = int(A) ∩ int(B).
solution: int(A)∩int(B) is open and contained in A∩B, so it is contained in int(A∩B). Conversely int(A∩B) is open and contained in A, hence in int(A); likewise in int(B); so int(A∩B)⊆int(A)∩int(B). Equality follows.

statement: Let B be a basis for a topology on X. Prove that a set U is open if and only if for every x in U there is a basis element B with x ∈ B ⊆ U.
solution: By definition the topology generated by B consists of unions of basis elements. If U is such a union then each x∈U lies in some basis element B⊆U. Conversely if every point of U has a basis element inside U, then U is the union of those basis elements, hence open.

statement: Prove that in a topology generated by a basis B, every open set is a union of basis elements.
solution: Let U be open. By b11, for each x∈U pick a basis element B_x with x∈B_x⊆U. Then U=∪_{x∈U} B_x, a union of basis elements.

statement: Prove that a subset D of X is dense (cl(D) = X) if and only if every nonempty open set meets D.
solution: cl(D)=X iff every point of X is in cl(D) iff every open nbhd of every point meets D (b04) iff every nonempty open set meets D.

statement: Prove that in the discrete topology every subset is both open and closed.
solution: In the discrete topology every subset is open by definition. Given any subset A, its complement X\A is also a subset, hence open, so A is closed. Thus every subset is clopen.

statement: On an infinite set X with the finite-complement topology, prove that the closed sets are exactly the finite subsets together with X.
solution: By definition U is open iff U=∅ or X\U is finite. Taking complements, C is closed iff C=X or C is finite. So the closed sets are precisely the finite subsets and X itself.

statement: Prove that in a T1 space every finite subset is closed.
solution: In a T1 space singletons {x} are closed. A finite set is a finite union of singletons, and a finite union of closed sets is closed, so every finite set is closed.

statement: Prove that cl(A ∩ B) ⊆ cl(A) ∩ cl(B).
solution: A∩B⊆A gives cl(A∩B)⊆cl(A) (b07); similarly cl(A∩B)⊆cl(B). Intersecting, cl(A∩B)⊆cl(A)∩cl(B).

statement: Let A be a subspace of X. Prove that a set is open in A if and only if it has the form A ∩ U for some U open in X.
solution: This is the definition of the subspace topology: the open sets of A are exactly {A∩U : U open in X}. One checks this collection is a topology (closed under arbitrary unions and finite intersections because U↦A∩U preserves them), which is the subspace topology on A.

statement: Prove that a set A is closed if and only if it contains all of its limit points.
solution: cl(A)=A ∪ A' where A' is the set of limit points (b05/a14). A is closed iff A=cl(A) iff A⊇A', i.e. A contains all its limit points.

statement: Prove that the collection of open intervals (a,b) with rational endpoints is a basis for the standard topology on R.
solution: Each rational-endpoint interval is open in R. Given any open U and x∈U, there is ε>0 with (x-ε,x+ε)⊆U; choose rationals p,q with x-ε<p<x<q<x+ε, so x∈(p,q)⊆U. By b11 this collection is a basis, and it generates the standard topology since its elements are standard-open and every standard-open set is such a union.
